op:Lib.image.color.ColorGrade.note: A five-minute introduction to color grading in Tooll, centered on the lift/gamma/gain controls of the ColorGrade operator, reading the WaveForm operator's scope, and comparing before/after with CompareImages.

Push highlights warm and shadows cool for the cinematic "pop" look; the gain/bias control is a contrast curve you drag left/right (steepen into an S for more contrast, flatten for less) and up/down to shift it, like a Photoshop curve in two parameters.

Lift/gamma/gain is the core of pro color grading: lift moves shadows, gamma the midtones, gain the highlights, each neutral at gray; push gain down and midtones up to add contrast, and tint each band toward a hue for a teal-and-orange look. Includes a vignette band with its own radius.
Why raising gamma brightens darks toward each other while a low gamma deepens them — the non-obvious reason a graded image can look "inverted" before you adjust brightness.
Push brightness and tune the overall look to set scene mood; can be dialed in by feel rather than by exact values.
Image effects don't overwrite their input; TiXL allocates a fresh same-size buffer for the result so the untouched original is still available downstream (e.g. to recombine with a glow pass).
Where most of a scene's final look is set — start from a preset or hand-tune curves to push the overall mood after geometry and lighting are done.

ui:ProjectSettings.note: A tip walkthrough explaining why all time in Tooll runs in bars rather than seconds, how to add a soundtrack to a project and dial in its BPM rate so procedural animation stays synced.

Export requires wrapping the graph into a symbol with a texture output (the root level can't have outputs) because the player derives resolution from it; title, author, and the new strip-unused-operators option live in the project's executable settings, and an export button now works from inside the project.

Redesigned per-project playback/audio: enable playback settings, pick soundtrack vs. live-performance mode, set BPM and a sync offset for tracks that don't start on the downbeat, and choose bars/seconds/frames for the timeline ruler; live mode adds tap-tempo VJ playback and external MIDI-clock sync.

The background soundtrack moved out of the composition settings onto the timeline itself: drag the audio in, set it to background mode (or the locked background-image display), and use a negative clip offset instead of the removed soundtrack-offset setting.

op:Lib.image.fx.feedback.AdvancedFeedbac.note: A deep walkthrough of the AdvancedFeedback effect: how its displace-along-a-slope feedback loop works internally, and a guided tour of nearly every parameter (twist, displacement, sample distance, shade, blur, color shifts, amplified edges, limit brights) and how to drive them for smoke-, water- and reaction-diffusion-like looks.

op:Lib.io.osc.OscInput.note: How to drive live visuals from a phone or tablet over OSC: [OscInput] auto-detects the address of any control you touch (the built-in teach mode), multiple inputs on the same port share one connection for free, and its float output can be split into X/Y/pressure to paint feedback trails whose color and line breaks follow the incoming pressure. A practical walkthrough of wiring a TouchOSC-style device into a generative drawing patch.

op:Lib.render.camera.OrbitCamera.note: A short tip walking through the parameters of the RandomCamera operator for procedural camera moves, plus how to drive its seed and shake inputs from a beat counter and noise.
Frame an instanced scene by orbiting around its center, then lower the camera to find a flattering angle on the surface.
Rotating with the middle mouse used to silently change the distance between camera position and target, breaking saved camera animations; a fix keeps that distance fixed while orbiting.

op:Lib.string.logic.PickStringPart.note: A short tip-of-the-day walkthrough showing how to split a text into lines/words/characters and step through the fragments to animate text, then pointing to a simpler random-string shortcut.

op:Lib.io.audio.AudioReaction.note: A short tip showing how to feed external audio into the graph and use [AudioReaction] to drive a particle scene — clearing the background and re-seeding randomness on each beat, and steering camera and noise with the level output.
Pick an audio input device, set its gain via the level meter, then create this op and connect it to a scene to drive audio-reactive effects; the chosen device/gain is stored per project.

ui:RenderSettings.note: A short tip explaining how an image operator's resolution is resolved: the "magic" 0×0 default pulls resolution from an incoming texture if present, otherwise from the output window, and how -1 or an explicit size overrides that.

Geometry draw operators expose a hardware blend mode (normal/additive/invert…) that controls how the drawn pixels combine with what's already in the render target — additive on a black background reads as transparent, but a correct multiply isn't available there.
Video export gained audio output, no pre-render format conversion, and an auto-increment version-number checkbox so you can re-hit render with the panel docked to save numbered work steps.

op:Lib.point.combine.CombineBuffers.note: A short tip showing that each point operator emits its own GPU point buffer, and how keeping the original and modified buffers around lets you wire them together — pairing positions to draw lines, then scattering meshes across the same points.

op:Lib.field.render.RaymarchField.note: A guided tour of TiXL's new SDF/field shader-graph system: the four operator categories (generators, space, adjust, combine), how ray-marching renders fields, performance and aliasing trade-offs, and using fields to drive particle forces and point selection.

Swap an SDF's default shader-graph rendering for this to gain ambient-occlusion shading; its AO-distance knob adds contact shadow the cheaper path lacks. Pick it when you want the SDF surface to read as solid.
A quick ray-march scene: feed it an SDF field and set a hard, glossy material to get a clean reflective sphere to test variable-driven parameters against.
Why raising the normal-sampling distance softens the surface — it blurs the sampled normals so a low-res source height map reads smoother instead of pixel-stepped.
A view-direction bug in the PBR specular term made mesh and ray-marched-field surfaces shade differently; unifying the PBR shading into a shared include keeps both paths visually aligned.

To detect externally when an SDF finished compiling, grab the raymarcher's second output (the generated shader-code string) and write it to a file as a completion signal — though file writing currently fails outside permitted paths under the new asset pipeline, logged as a to-do.
Colorizing a field in the final colorization pass is far cheaper than during ray-marching, because the color is evaluated once per pixel after the march completes rather than at every march step.

op:Lib.point.generate.PointTrail.note: A short tip showing how to feed animated, noise-displaced points into a cyclic trail buffer to draw streaking trails, then layer extra noise and fog on the result.
Records past point positions to draw motion trails; reworked to be more consistent and to avoid gaps in the lines, though its interpolation is still not perfectly smooth.

op:Lib.render.utils.RequestedResolution.note: A short tip explaining how an image operator's resolution is resolved: the "magic" 0×0 default pulls resolution from an incoming texture if present, otherwise from the output window, and how -1 or an explicit size overrides that.

op:Lib.render.analyze.GetScreenPos.note: A tip-of-the-day walkthrough of the new [GetScreenPos] operator (TiXL 4.0.2), which converts a world-space locator into a 2D screen-space coordinate so a label or billboard can be pinned over a point in a post-processed 3D scene.

ui:TimeOverrides.note: A short tip on overriding the time that drives an animation: wrap a rendered texture in a command-time operator and feed it a custom time signal (a sine, a remapped random, a beat) to scrub, loop, or jump regions of a timeline non-linearly.

A walkthrough of TimeClips: how clips on the timeline gate which parts of a graph get evaluated per scene, and how dragging or stretching a clip remaps the time fed into its sub-graph, with the colour cues (orange/red) that signal time remapping and time-scaling.

op:Lib.numbers.anim.time.SetTime.note: A short tip on overriding the time that drives an animation: wrap a rendered texture in a command-time operator and feed it a custom time signal (a sine, a remapped random, a beat) to scrub, loop, or jump regions of a timeline non-linearly.
Freezes or remaps the playhead for everything drawn after it, so you can drive a sub-scene's animation from any value (e.g. a wave) and play that segment deterministically forward and backward.

Build a manual preloading screen: wrap the whole demo in a branch, animate a sweep 0→100 so every shader/clip is touched and pre-compiled behind a cover layer, then cut to live time. (As of 4.1 the player does this automatically.)
Render one scene twice with offset clocks: duplicate the group, feed each copy a different time so the same deterministic animation appears at two phases at once.
How remapping local time upstream changes what an operator reads as "now": feed it a looped/offset value and downstream time-driven nodes follow that remapped clock.

op:Lib.mesh.draw.DrawMeshAtPoints.note: Opening tip in a points series: explains the eight-value point structure (position, weight W, quaternion orientation), pushes a point list to a GPU buffer, then instances a mesh onto every point and shows how W and randomization drive the result.

A short tip contrasting two ways to multiply a mesh across scattered points: baking copies into one large mesh (cloning) versus drawing the same mesh repeatedly per point (instancing), and the trade-offs in memory, performance, and what you can still modify afterward.
Scatter a mesh (here a cylinder as a sprinkle) across a point set; it's the auto-suggested op when you connect points to a mesh, and it instances the geometry at every position.

Used to teach point attributes — instancing a cube at each point shows that a point carries far more than position (color, size, rotation), since rotation only becomes visible once you instance an oriented mesh on it.
Another consumer of the shared color field: scale instances down and drive their surface color from the same field as the rest of the scene.
Render a cylinder along each solved bone so an IK chain reads as a jointed robot limb instead of bare points; transform the mesh to align its long axis first.
Swap raw points for actual geometry by instancing a mesh at every point; the point set supplies position while a separate mesh input supplies the shape stamped at each one.

when no point buffer is connected the drawing falls back to a single point at the origin, and with one connected you can read the point index per fragment and sample any point attribute from a code snippet.

op:Lib.flow.TimeClip.note: A walkthrough of TimeClips: how clips on the timeline gate which parts of a graph get evaluated per scene, and how dragging or stretching a clip remaps the time fed into its sub-graph, with the colour cues (orange/red) that signal time remapping and time-scaling.

Plain dragging a time clip moves only its enable-window, not the keyframes inside; Alt-drag instead and it time-remaps, stretching or compressing the inner animation's local time — powerful but very easy to get lost in.
A time clip only gates whether its connected branch is visible during its span on the timeline; vertical order is irrelevant, it must be wired into something, and on its own it does nothing.

The remapped time-clip drives a child's local time from 0→1 over its window, and that same local time feeds the child's internal keyframes — the basis for reusable, retimeable chapter/title animations.

op:Lib.image.fx.stylize.Steps.note: A short scripted tip showing how the [Steps] image effect posterizes a gradient into bands, then animating it by wiring counters and an LFO into its offset, gradient rotation, and highlight color.

op:Lib.render.shading.SetRequestedResolu.note: A short tip explaining how an image operator's resolution is resolved: the "magic" 0×0 default pulls resolution from an incoming texture if present, otherwise from the output window, and how -1 or an explicit size overrides that.

Overrides the requested resolution carried in the context: positive values force a fixed size for all downstream 0,0 operators, negative values fall back to the output window, letting a post chain ignore an odd incoming image size.

op:Lib.image.generate.pattern.Raster.note: A short tip walking through the versatile Raster operator: its presets and knobs, then driving it from an input texture and stacking offset copies into a CMYK-style halftone print effect.
Give it an explicit resolution to draw a crisp high-res overlay on top of a deliberately low-res background image, decoupling the effect's detail from the source's pixel count.

ui:ShaderGraph.note: A guided tour of TiXL's new SDF/field shader-graph system: the four operator categories (generators, space, adjust, combine), how ray-marching renders fields, performance and aliasing trade-offs, and using fields to drive particle forces and point selection.

End-to-end of authoring a point-modifier shader op: duplicate a similar op as a new type, "edit" its generated shader to open the source, set p.color to a constant first to confirm you're in the right shader, then strip the unneeded mapping/noise branches.

Image effects build on an ImageFX-Static template (cacheable, nothing animated); add a parameter via right-click add-input, convert it to int/float, route it into the params buffer, then edit the fragment shader — clone the repo for read-write access to library operators.

Run TiXL in Debug from the IDE and capture a frame with RenderDoc (Ctrl+Shift+F12) to inspect each draw's bound shader, textures, and constant-buffer values — the fastest way to see what isn't bound or is mis-packed in a custom shader.

File > New scaffolds an image effect from a template, copying needed resources into your namespace and opening the shader in your editor; VS Code with the HLSL Tools extension is recommended for highlighting, autocomplete, and error squiggles.

When writing a C# operator's value you assign through the output slot's value (the slot also tracks dirty/update state) rather than returning directly — return a constant first to confirm hot-reload is live.

op:Lib.image.fx.feedback.AdvancedFeedbac.note: A deep walkthrough of the AdvancedFeedback effect: how its displace-along-a-slope feedback loop works internally, and a guided tour of nearly every parameter (twist, displacement, sample distance, shade, blur, color shifts, amplified edges, limit brights) and how to drive them for smoke-, water- and reaction-diffusion-like looks.

op:Lib.image.generate.pattern.Rings.note: A short tip tour of the [Rings] operator, walking every parameter that shapes its concentric-ring pattern and pointing out which ones reward animation.

ui:Timeline.note: A short tip on snapping keyframes precisely in the timeline: pinning parameters, switching the ruler from seconds to bars/beats/ticks, and using ALT to scale and insert keyframes onto snap targets.

The rewritten dope-sheet adds a drag handle on the time region, shaded value backgrounds for scanning, and post/pre extrapolation per keyframe selection (cycle, cycle-with-offset to step the value up or down each repeat) for endless loops.

Tangents now default to a fast fixed-length spline (Kochanek/Hermite-style); hold Ctrl or Ctrl+Shift to lengthen a handle and switch that key to a fully expressive cubic spline, and snap a handle flat to flip it to linear.
Two clips that overlap in time are rendered in order and crossfaded, giving a proper blend between adjacent shots.

The background soundtrack moved out of the composition settings onto the timeline itself: drag the audio in, set it to background mode (or the locked background-image display), and use a negative clip offset instead of the removed soundtrack-offset setting.

Drag an mp3 straight onto the timeline to load it as an audio clip with computed spectrum; multiple parallel audio tracks (no longer one fixed soundtrack) move TiXL toward video-editing-style layering.
Scrubbing with the left mouse jumps playback; releasing lets time continue forward from that point, which lets you preview a moment then keep rolling.
New time clips auto-stack to avoid overlap, and Ctrl+X splits a clip at the playhead while re-wiring the new half into the same group — much faster than hand-editing overlapping clips.
Keyframes don't auto-snap to the grid, but the background grid is driven by the project's BPM/FPS so you can snap the outer keys to it, select all, and "space evenly" to lock a sequence to the beat.
Tap a beat live by holding Alt and pressing Shift+C to drop keyframes in time with music; polyrhythmic tracks won't land evenly, which is what the redistribute tool then fixes.

ui:OutputWindow.note: A short tip showing the Save Screenshot button, which writes the current output frame at full resolution to the `.t3/screenshots` folder.
In fill mode the viewer matches its window's vertical extent and pads left/right to the set aspect ratio, so dragging the panel reflows the view without distorting it.

a command-type operator's primary output executes rendering, but pinning its secondary source-code output in a dedicated output view is the practical way to debug "undefined symbol" errors, and the included PBR formula lives in the PbrRenderer HLSL include if you need to read the actual math.

op:Lib.point.sim.SimNoiseOffset.note: A short tip showing how to feed animated, noise-displaced points into a cyclic trail buffer to draw streaking trails, then layer extra noise and fog on the result.

op:Lib.image.generate.basic.RenderTarget.note: A short tip explaining how an image operator's resolution is resolved: the "magic" 0×0 default pulls resolution from an incoming texture if present, otherwise from the output window, and how -1 or an explicit size overrides that.

Feed it a camera and the magic 0,0 resolution to capture a scene into a texture, then crank the texture to 8K to watch pixel count (and effect cost) explode — this is where a heavy post chain actually gets paid for, in millions of pixels per frame.
Add a second texture output to a wrapped operator (right-click → add output, set type to texture), then a 2D layer lets you place that rendered image as a plane in 3D space.
Its 0,0 resolution makes a sub-scene render at whatever size the consumer asks for, so the same graph is sharp at 480p or 8k without edits.
Piping into a 32-bit (float) render target instead of 8-bit makes a large visible quality difference for accumulated/feedback-style effects.

op:Lib.point.generate.PointTrailFast.note: A short tip showing how to feed animated, noise-displaced points into a cyclic trail buffer to draw streaking trails, then layer extra noise and fog on the result.

ui:DopeSheet.note: A short tip on snapping keyframes precisely in the timeline: pinning parameters, switching the ruler from seconds to bars/beats/ticks, and using ALT to scale and insert keyframes onto snap targets.
Hold Alt to drop warp points inside a selected range, then stretch the interior non-uniformly to retime a block of keyframes without moving its ends.
Right-click a keyframe layer and "set sequential values" (start at 0 or 1) to renumber a row of index keys cleanly instead of leaving them at fractional in-between values.

By default it only shows keyframes of selected operators; the new auto-pin mode keeps every animated parameter visible while you jump between ops, and Shift+K clears the pinned set to start a fresh animation group.

Copy keyframes and paste them onto any other animated parameter; paste lands the first key at the current time, and for a multi-channel target you must rename/select the matching X/Y curves so the pasted channels map correctly.

op:Lib.point.modify.SelectPoints.note: Write a 0/1 mask into F1/F2 from whether a point sits inside a shape; the SDF variant binds the test to any distance field (a torus, noise-displaced) instead of the legacy fixed sphere, making it far more expressive as a selector.
Enable its gizmo to drag the selection region through the cloud live; scale, stretch and rotate the region to reshape what gets selected.
Pair a point selection with a transform so a squeeze only affects points inside the selected volume, leaving the rest untouched.
Switch the volume shape from sphere to plane and rotate it to get a directional falloff band; the bias softens the selection edge for a smoother transition.

op:Lib.image.use.BlendWithMask.note: Feed a [LinearGradient] as the mask to make blur fall off across the frame; align the gradient angle (here ~131°) and use ping-pong to blur both edges while keeping the center sharp.
Use plain [Blend] when you just want A over B; reach for the mask variant only when a separate image should gate where the blend happens.

op:Lib.image.generate.basic.LinearGradie.note: Feed a [LinearGradient] as the mask to make blur fall off across the frame; align the gradient angle (here ~131°) and use ping-pong to blur both edges while keeping the center sharp.

Sample separate color channels of a scrolling ping-pong gradient to drive different point transforms at once (red to Z-offset, green to rotation); switch its interpolation from linear to smooth to kill the stepped, non-moving look.
Sample colours straight off a reference with Alt-click to recreate its background; flip the gradient direction if the picked endpoints come out reversed.
Size-mode "align to height" vs. "align to width" decides which axis the gradient spans as the canvas aspect changes; align-to-height keeps a circle drawn over it perfectly round at any resolution.

op:Lib.render.shading.PointLight.note: Prefer it over SetPointLight: it wraps the same setup but also draws a gizmo sphere you can grab and move in the viewport; the specular term was previously computed from the wrong light position and is now corrected.
Raise decay (≈6) so falloff stays near the source instead of washing out distant elements, then balance intensity (≈5) and tint the light for mood.
A second light placed off to one side in a contrasting color adds rim/fill separation; brighten it to gauge its effect, then pull intensity back down.

A default scene already has lighting on so beginners see something; create a point light for full control, but the still-lit far side comes from indirect/environment light, not this op. Order between point lights doesn't matter — last eight win.

Ctrl-click a position parameter to extract it as a shared input you can feed to both a light and your shader offset, add a gizmo for on-screen handles, and note that all scene lights are already available in the shader as a Lights[] structure array you can index directly.

op:Lib.point.modify.SelectPointsWithSDF.note: Feed a CustomSDF in and write the selection to an FX attribute; that attribute then drives anything per-point — here emit speed from a grid into a ParticleSystem, varying by region of the field.

Write a 0/1 mask into F1/F2 from whether a point sits inside a shape; the SDF variant binds the test to any distance field (a torus, noise-displaced) instead of the legacy fixed sphere, making it far more expressive as a selector.

The range mapping modes (centered / from-start / ping-pong / repeat) plus gain-bias decide how a field's distance maps onto the 0..1 selection; zero distance reads as maximum selection, and the strength factor lets a second selection localize the effect.
Used as the template to clone from when building a sibling point-field op, since both walk a point buffer and sample a field per point.

op:Lib.point.generate.GridPoints.note: Lay out a flat grid of points and instance a cube at each to block out a city; raise the cube's pivot to its base so the points sit at ground level and scaling grows buildings upward instead of from their centre.
Generate a volumetric point cloud (e.g. 10×10×10) as the source for instanced quads; the per-point W value starts uniform and is what you later vary.

Cell mode keeps a fixed spacing between points as you add more; bounds mode instead fills a set volume by redistributing them — reach for cell when the gap matters, bounds when the extent matters. Drop the Y count to 1 for a flat layer.
Set one axis to a single point and the other two to 100 each to get a flat 100×100 sheet of points; scale the whole grid up to size the surface you'll instance onto.
Drop the per-axis count (e.g. 3×3) and tighten the scale to get a sparse, compact point set to scatter copies onto.

op:Lib.particle.force.TextureMapForce.note: Pulls particles toward bright areas of a signed normal map in screen space; twist the pull angle to swirl or (at 180°) repel, great for logo animations and combinable with 2D image effects like reaction-diffusion.

A *screen-space* force: render a layer to a texture, derive a normal map, and push a particle system away from bright areas — easy to art-direct but breaks for 360° output because the push is camera-plane aligned.

Accelerates particles along a connected normal map (which must use signed-normal mode); a twist parameter rotates the sampled direction — 180° reverses it — and a confine-depth parameter keeps particles within a visible distance from the camera.

op:Lib.particle.ParticleSystem.note: A long-lifetime, zero-emit-velocity emitter seeded once per beat hit: each emission re-seeds, particles live ~40s, and the age attribute drives a gradient so they glow then fade.

Lifetime reworked: a default of -1 derives the max lifetime from emitted-point count and buffer length, and particle age written to the w attribute is now normalized 0–1 so you can drive color or scale over a particle's life.
The new Emit Velocity Factor scales launch speed; switching emit mode from sequential to lines lets DrawLines render the trails as shaded ribbons.
Emit count appends into a ring buffer up to max-particle-count, so you can freely vary or animate how many points you emit per frame to grow particle complexity over time.

Emit velocity has a non-zero default (like Unity) so particles visibly move out of the box; zero it for neutral-force setups. The emit-velocity-factor reads an emitter attribute (e.g. F1) so you can shoot some emitters fast and leave others static.

correct transparency requires drawing back-to-front because the per-pixel write-depth-or-not decision is binary, so a fading sprite must cut off somewhere; order-independent transparency exists but needs a heavy multi-render-target setup comparable to screen-space ambient occlusion.

internally a fixed-size ring buffer where unused slots are NaN "separator" points that drawing ops skip; the emit cursor wraps around overwriting the oldest particles, the emit count can change freely per frame, and multiple simultaneous emits are distributed across the buffer rather than written as one chunk.
Never drive max-particle-count from a per-frame-changing value: reallocating a large GPU buffer every frame fragments VRAM and can crash; only change buffer size in coarse steps.

trail length from chained systems is the ratio of the second buffer to the first (1000 upstream into 5000 gives 5-point trails), and attribute mapping for grow-and-fade over lifetime keeps working on the re-emitted particles.

Speed multiplies how much of each particle's velocity is applied per frame, so you can slow, freeze, or briefly reverse motion — but it only affects velocity-based forces, not ones that move position directly.
Source points and live particles are different buffers, so a value must be written into the particle at emission to survive into the render — you can't just read it from the seed points afterward.

Relative cost budgeting for a particle scene: drawing the points with supersampling dominates (~100 units), the sim itself ~10, a 3D-noise turbulence force ~15, a texture-sampling force ~10, a directional force ~2 — so optimize the draw before the forces.

It needs input points plus at least one force or it stays empty; internally it builds a particle buffer (carrying velocity) separate from the result point buffer, since particles need acceleration that plain points don't.
Drag removes a fixed percentage of velocity each frame (scaled by speed), needed because forces like turbulence keep pumping energy in and would otherwise make the system explode.
Disabling its Update freezes the whole simulation for inspection, and is also how you pre-warm particles then hold the result as a static abstract scene.
Set max-particle-count to -1 to size the buffer to the emit set, then emit only on a beat boolean to spawn a fixed batch and keep it alive indefinitely.

op:Lib.mesh.draw.DrawMesh.note: DrawMesh now accepts a field: convert an SDF/plane field through SdfToColor and feed it as the color input to paint a procedural color map onto mesh surfaces, consistent with the SDF render path.
The statistically most common follow-up when you click a mesh-buffer output; TiXL ranks connection suggestions by how people actually wire that output type.
Build a small cylinder, reduce its segment detail and shrink its radius/height, then draw it stacked on a cube to compose a Lego-style brick from primitives.
Pair a primitive mesh with a draw operator to make geometry visible in the output; shrink the mesh radius before composing it with other shapes.
A view-direction bug in the PBR specular term made mesh and ray-marched-field surfaces shade differently; unifying the PBR shading into a shared include keeps both paths visually aligned.

Backface culling explained: by default only front faces draw (as little as necessary for real-time), so a flat plane vanishes from behind — switch the cull side or disable culling to make it double-sided.

ui:VariationWindow.note: Snapshot vs. preset: a snapshot is stored on the operator's own symbol and saved into it, while a preset stores the instance parameters into the composition that uses the operator — same blending mechanism, different owner.

How per-parameter snapshots work: instead of flagging a whole operator, right-click individual parameters to expose only those to a snapshot, then capture/recall named states from the empty-input background view.
As of 4.2 snapshots and variations live in a per-project meta folder (thumbnails plus data) instead of the global roaming settings, so that folder must be kept and backed up.
Why the per-parameter capture stays flat by default: an earlier prototype prompted for a snapshot group every time, but 99% of uses needed only one group, so grouping was dropped for speed.
Step or blend between saved states with cursor keys or an index input, so a cycling integer animation walks through presets live.
Select an effect, choose which of its parameters to vary, and generate random variations with adjustable randomization strength; any result you like is saveable as a preset.

op:Lib.point.modify.MapPointAttributes.note: To invert a particle's F1 factor, set its input/output mode to F1 and draw a 0→1 / 1→0 curve in the built-in curve editor; ping-pong and phase modes let an F value repeat a pattern over time.

A meta-mapper that binds a chosen source (buffer order, F1/F2, random, particle age) to a target (color via gradient, scale, fade) — e.g. colorize points by the F1 mask an upstream SDF wrote, with a multiply color mode that's neutral at 1.
Map a selection attribute (F1) to color so a hand-crafted field paints specific regions of a particle effect — e.g. turn one zone blue.
Write particle age into F1 (0→1) then drive a gradient lookup from it to colorize particles over their lifetime.

trail length from chained systems is the ratio of the second buffer to the first (1000 upstream into 5000 gives 5-point trails), and attribute mapping for grow-and-fade over lifetime keeps working on the re-emitted particles.

op:Lib.particle.force.ReconstructiveForc.note: Pulls scattered particles back toward an arbitrary target point set within a spherical volume — letting them dissolve into chaos then reform into a logo/shape; ideal candidate for field support.
Drives particles toward an arbitrary target point set — e.g. replicated grid points randomized into an abstract structure — to reform them into a shape.

op:Lib.point.modify.CustomPointShader.note: The shader alternative to factor remapping: write `pfx1 = 1 - pfx1` to invert a factor, and wrap it in `saturate()` to clamp 0–1 so tiny values don't go negative.

Insert it after drawing points to run an on-the-fly compiled GPU snippet per point; each point exposes an f variable running 0→1 across the set, and writing to position gives sine displacement while writing to the w attribute yields a wave-shaped field—fast enough for millions of points.

Carry a value from emission into a particle by writing it to fx2 (fx1 already holds age) at the emit shader, then reading fx2 in the draw shader — the pattern for "tag each particle at birth and recall it later," since emitter and particle buffers are otherwise separate.
`getFieldNormal(position)` plus `RotateToFace`/look-at the normal orients instanced meshes to the field surface; swapping the normal's component order picks which mesh axis aligns to it.

Adding a field input: the field/SDF call and its texture must be registered at the right contiguous register slot (after the int params), and multi-input resources after it shift the count — a binding-order constraint when extending the shader.

Exposes f as each point's normalized 0..1 position in the buffer and t as frac(f) shaped by a built-in bias/gain helper, so stretching or biasing that curve reshapes value distribution or acts as a threshold, and adding an offset before frac() cycles the mapping.
Orient-to-SDF preset: read distance for colour via [SampleGradient], read the field normal to rotate, and drive scale by `1/(abs(distance)+1)` so points balloon near the surface.

Recolor an existing point buffer (e.g. a global hue shift for DMX fixtures) with a small shader stage that rewrites each point's color — there is no stock operator for this, and offsetting points to resample a texture is clumsier.
Write a vertex/point's own position into an fx attribute (`pfx1 = p.position.x`) so a downstream stage can read coordinates back as data — a general "stash a value per point" trick.

op:Lib.render.camera.ReuseCamera.note: Pull a camera reference from a camera operator's extra output and replay it on a second sub-scene so both render from the identical viewpoint, then composite them (one edge-detected, one plain) in post.

To build a fisheye/distortion rig without breaking projections, copy this node and set the reference as an object transform rather than as the active camera, so the matrix rotates geometry instead of replacing the view.

op:Lib.io.midi.MidiInput.note: Live MIDI/OSC input can be recorded into clips and later replayed to emulate the same named device, so a teach-enabled input downstream re-learns from the recorded events exactly as if the controller were live.
after plugging in a controller, rescan devices in settings; the first physical slider movement teaches the mapping to the connected parameter, then adjust the output range to fit.

op:Lib.point.modify.MoveToSDF.note: Snap a scattered point cloud onto a surface by feeding it the points and an SDF field — the way to plant sprinkles on a torus; follow it with point-space transforms to align and randomise the now-surface-bound instances.
Distributes grid points onto an SDF surface (e.g. a smooth-combined sphere "monkey"); move the source points and they redistribute, then draw a mesh at each to clad the shape.

op:Lib.particle.force.FieldVolumeForce.note: To bounce falling particles outward off a floor, bump the plane SDF with an added sphere and set attraction to zero so reflection scatters them sideways.

The powerful SDF-driven force: separate attraction (outside) and repulsion (inside) with adjustable decay, plus surface-bounce reflection with randomizable bounciness; invert the volume to trap particles inside a shape like a container.

The SDF-based sibling of the mesh collider: same parameters minus normal-sampling distance, and because a box SDF's distance is far more consistent than a mesh's per-face distance it gives smoother, more reliable repulsion.
Now superset of FieldDistanceForce, with reflect-on-collision and apply-color-on-collision options that sample the SDF's color onto colliding points.

op:Lib.numbers.anim.animators.TriggerAni.note: Build a "trigger keyframe" you don't have natively: step an animated value up with Shift+C per key, floor it to an int, and feed change-detection into a one-shot animation so each step fires an event.
Feed its pulse into a randomized phase so each beat re-rolls point positions; cleaner than wiring AnimValue for the same job.

op:Lib.image.generate.noise.FractalNoise.note: Feed a noise field into the attribute sampler to push point positions along a single axis, turning a flat grid into a rolling surface; rotate the noise 90° and raise its scaling so the pattern aligns with the grid plane.
Offset and warp-offset values shift where the noise samples, and animating those (rather than the underlying field) is enough to make the displaced surface drift like water.

op:Lib.particle.force.DirectionalForce.note: To bounce falling particles outward off a floor, bump the plane SDF with an added sphere and set attraction to zero so reflection scatters them sideways.
A constant directional push (gravity by default), combinable additively with other forces; its visible gizmo just orients arrow indicators along the direction.

ui:SkillQuestLevel.note: Building a level: the reference output, the editable "solution" feeding it, and disconnected building blocks the learner wires up; a step that says "connect X to the point's position" via tour points — beware a multiply-blend that lets the wrong wiring still pass.

op:Lib.mesh.generate.RepeatMeshAtPoints.note: A short tip contrasting two ways to multiply a mesh across scattered points: baking copies into one large mesh (cloning) versus drawing the same mesh repeatedly per point (instancing), and the trade-offs in memory, performance, and what you can still modify afterward.

Lay out a flat grid of points and instance a cube at each to block out a city; raise the cube's pivot to its base so the points sit at ground level and scaling grows buildings upward instead of from their centre.
Wire a points set into one input and a mesh into the other to stamp a copy of the mesh at every point; chain it after the points generator that defines the layout.

op:Lib.image.use.CustomPixelShader.note: The fastest way to learn shader work: it hands you an HLSL stub that must return color C (default white, an RGBA vector); read UV from 0,0 bottom-left to 1,1, and sample one of the built-in gradient/image inputs to map position or a parameter to color.

After declaring frequency/amplitude params in the buffer at the top of the file, add a sine offset to the UV coordinates to get a live displacement; nothing moves until amplitude is raised above zero.
Inside hand-written shader code the real hazard is an unrolled for-loop: a huge fixed count can crash the app, so every loop should carry a hard maximum.

The low-level path: a pixel/vertex-shader-stage helper sets shaders, constant buffers, samplers and resources, runs the draw, then restores the previous GPU state — copy an ImageFX effect's innards here to go fully manual.

extra textures can reach a mesh shader by hijacking unused material slots (e.g. emissive) via the material operator, or via a multi-input plus additional-defines pattern, until a dedicated image input exists.

op:Lib.numbers.int.logic.HasIntChanged.note: Build a "trigger keyframe" you don't have natively: step an animated value up with Shift+C per key, floor it to an int, and feed change-detection into a one-shot animation so each step fires an event.

op:Lib.flow.context.GetFloatVar.note: Name a variable once, then read it back anywhere with the matching getter so one source (a noise, a MIDI value, a master volume) drives many places; the setter only exists where its subgraph runs, so wire it under an [Execute] pinned first to guarantee it evaluates before its readers.
Reads a named float set elsewhere with auto-completion from context, letting you reuse one driving value (e.g. an intensity) anywhere in a large project.

op:Lib.flow.context.SetFloatVar.note: Place it first inside an Execute, name the variable, and share one value across many effects; hovering shows highlighted lines to every reader of that variable.

Name a variable once, then read it back anywhere with the matching getter so one source (a noise, a MIDI value, a master volume) drives many places; the setter only exists where its subgraph runs, so wire it under an [Execute] pinned first to guarantee it evaluates before its readers.

op:Lib.numbers.anim.vj.SetSpeedFactors.note: Pin it at the start of a chain to override the global time factors A and B; map a MIDI knob to a factor and everything time-driven downstream speeds up or slows together for live tempo ramps and breakdowns.

op:Lib.numbers.bool.process.DelayTrigger.note: Holds a one-frame trigger open for a set duration so a particle emitter fires across several frames instead of one; also debounces rapid double-triggers down to a single emission.

op:Lib.numbers.color.BuildGradient.note: Builds a gradient procedurally from a color list plus an overridable position list — feed a PlaybackFFT (or any float list) into the positions to make an audio-reactive gradient for displacement and color.

op:Lib.image.color.ColorGradeDepth.note: Feeds the depth buffer alongside the image so a gradient grades by distance — e.g. tinting the background cooler — for subtle, very effective atmospheric depth cueing.

op:Lib.render.shading.SetMaterial.note: In a stack the last material wins: evaluation is pull-based from the output backwards, so a material lower (later) in the stack overrides earlier ones — set a default then override one object.
Set the base color to a gradient and rotate it 90° to shade ribbons across their width instead of along their length.
A quick ray-march scene: feed it an SDF field and set a hard, glossy material to get a clean reflective sphere to test variable-driven parameters against.
Works on both meshes and SDFs; lowering glossiness moves a surface from shiny toward a frosted matte look, and bypassing it shows the bare default shading underneath.
Drive emissive color plus a high luminance (e.g. 10) for a self-lit glowing surface, or lower roughness and raise metalness for a reflective metal look.

extra textures can reach a mesh shader by hijacking unused material slots (e.g. emissive) via the material operator, or via a multi-input plus additional-defines pattern, until a dedicated image input exists.
A faint dark-blue emissive on a neutral material reads as distant water — a small emissive tint shifts perceived color without lighting the scene.

op:Lib.image.fx.stylize.Glow.note: It barely glows until the source is actually HDR: push a color's brightness above 1 (Ctrl-drag the color past white) and the glow then spreads that over-bright energy across the image.
Beyond intensity, its glow-gradient knob colour-tints the bloom by brightness, letting the bright core read one hue and the soft falloff another.
Its default strength is deliberately very intense, so expect to dial it down — this is what makes bright/emissive materials bloom.

op:Lib.image.generate.basic.RoundedRect.note: Roundness 1 turns the rect into a circle and stroke-only (no fill/background) gives a ring; enabling its mip-map generation is what fixes the shimmer when the shape is later minified by a camera.
Composite a soft glowing shape over a scene by scaling a [Layer2d] down and feeding it a [RoundedRect]; crank feathering and tune the aspect ratio for the shape you need.

op:Lib.image.color.RemapColor.note: Maps each input colour through a gradient per-channel or in grayscale; a hold-interpolated step makes a threshold, and its own gain/bias positions where that threshold falls.

Maps an image's tonal range onto a gradient (black→left, white→right) and clamps at 1, so it fits LDR/after-glow stages but not HDR; Alt-pick colors straight from a reference image to match its palette.
A glue op between an input texture and a gradient: switch to spline interpolation and insert handles to reshape contrast like a Photoshop curves adjustment.

Invert a grayscale image fastest by swapping the dark and light target colors; the same two color anchors plus contrast controls also give quick teal-orange style grades, slightly cheaper than a full color remap.

ui:EvaluationContext.note: Parameter-input smoothing (default ~6 frames) softens every knob change, so changing a time-evaluated animation's rate "jumps" to where it should be — smoothing can't fix it because the value isn't accumulated.
Why TiXL splits work CPU-side (positions, sizes, names, file loading) from GPU-side (the buffers and textures it generates), and what that division costs you in flexibility.
What the Z-buffer is: a depth buffer parallel to the colour buffer that decides per-pixel whether something is drawn based on its distance from the camera plane.
A faded-out branch's per-frame CPU cost drops almost to nothing because it's no longer evaluated, but its cached buffers stay resident — the RAM it holds is not freed.
Refactoring a graph criss-crossed with long connections into per-frame context variables (booleans, ints, vectors) set once up front and read wherever needed downstream.

ui:Graph.note: A disconnected operator costs nothing — TiXL ignores anything not wired into the graph, so duplicating (Ctrl+D pastes at the mouse) a material as a safety copy has zero performance impact until you drag it into the stack.

Z-fighting (flickering where two coplanar surfaces meet) and its fixes: nudge one slightly up, or disable the depth test — but with the test off the object draws regardless of depth, so you must reorder it in the group's multi-input to control what ends up on top.
A maintainer's pull-request review workflow: small diff + operators-only changes (no editor/core) means low blast radius and a quick merge.
Control+Shift+D duplicates with connections, correctly handling multi-inputs, and shaking an operator out now reconnects all compatible inputs rather than just the first.
Horizontal snapping (Alt+A) aligns operators so the connection-line router knows they're related and keeps parallel wires from overlapping — subtle but it cleans up tangled graphs.
Operators no longer auto-disconnect when dragged out of a group (it broke graphs too often); you can still reorder within vertical/horizontal stacks, with connections temporary during the drag.

The three operator output colours encode where data lives: a texture lives on the GPU and is regenerated each time you modify it, a buffer is an opaque GPU pointer you can't read back but can draw from, and a green node is a draw/command. Knowing the colour tells you what an output can and can't do.

A multi-input (the angled socket) accepts any number of connections shown as blinking insertion points; wiring the same object twice into a group renders it twice, e.g. to build up opacity on a transparent object.
Image-comparison unit tests render convoluted scenes and flag a failure when output drifts; run them before each commit to catch rendering regressions across the PBR paths.
A fully static subtree caches and costs nothing; selecting an operator invalidates it (params might change) and breaks the cache, so deselect to let scenes settle.
Node text blurs when zoomed because ImGui draws every glyph as a textured quad from a fixed font atlas (only four font sizes); a future 2D-SDF font shader would make it crisp.
press Shift+B to bypass an operator in place instead of disconnecting it, which behaves like breaking the connection but is instantly reversible.

The magnetic graph: long-press selects a single op, long-press-and-drag plus a shake disconnects it, and dropping a node near a connection snaps it into a vertical stacked batch — clicking a stacked node then drags the whole stack.
In a vertical operator stack you can long-press-drag a member out of the chain, or drop a new one between two blinking insert lines to control exactly where in the render order it lands.
A non-obvious copy shortcut in the graph: single-click to grab a node's value/expression, then Ctrl+N to spin it into a new node — handy when refactoring inline code.

op:Lib.render.shading.SetEnvironment.note: Its order relative to the camera matters: it renders the background first, before the camera is known, so placing it after the camera (and with an opaque, non-transparent source image) is required for a consistent background — the image-based-lighting math fails on a transparent input.
An advanced "background blur" option blurs the environment backdrop independently of the depth-of-field on the geometry.
After assigning an environment texture you must trigger an "update live once" so the lighting actually samples the new cube map.

Supplies image-based / indirect lighting (HDRI-style); switch among built-in presets to relight the whole scene, set it to black to kill ambient, and toggle whether the environment itself is rendered as background.

op:Lib.point.draw.DrawPoints.note: AlphaCutoff decides when a fading sprite still writes depth: raising it toward fully opaque removes black outlines but hardens soft blurry textures, and fully transparent texture areas must keep the same RGB as the visible part or their color leaks into the blend.

correct transparency requires drawing back-to-front because the per-pixel write-depth-or-not decision is binary, so a fading sprite must cut off somewhere; order-independent transparency exists but needs a heavy multi-render-target setup comparable to screen-space ambient occlusion.
Render a point set as visible dots and add it into the scene group; reuse the same generator with a wider spread for a separate background layer.
enable GenerateMipMaps on large sprite textures so small distant particles both look better and render much faster, since fetched texture samples end up closer together in memory.

op:Lib.particle.force.TurbulenceForce.note: Frequency is really noise scale (high frequency = small scale); changing it live injects near-random jumps far from center, and floating-point drift slowly degrades any long-running turbulence into noise. Animate phase from a slowed time for gradual flow.
Record per-note audio volume into a keyframe track and pipe that envelope into a turbulence force so particle motion accelerates on louder notes.

keeps pushing at constant strength while drag tapers particle speed, so turbulence appears to grow dominant; some forces offer a use-particle-velocity-as-strength option and this one could gain it too.
Forces generally edit velocity, not age — so per-age effects aren't yet possible; discussed as the natural place for a future amount-from-attribute/field-graph driver.

op:Lib.numbers.float.random.PerlinNoise.note: For spin, feed noise into rotation and multiply its ±1 range up to 360°; lower frequency for slower turns and reduce octaves so the rotation holds a steady speed instead of jittering.
Wire a noise generator into a locator's position to make an object wander smoothly through space rather than follow a fixed path.
Tune the per-axis amplitude to constrain wandering motion to a plane — drop the vertical amplitude so the object circles rather than bobs up and down.

op:Lib.point.modify.RandomizePoints.note: Scatters points along their orientation (z = surface normal) and its gain/bias controls the distribution of the offset, so most points cluster at the outer shell while a few reach far, giving an animated shimmering surface.
Animate the random phase to keep points churning; pair with a color randomization for saturation/brightness jitter across the set.
Randomize a chosen point attribute (e.g. F1 used as scale) and shape the spread with gain/bias and a value curve so only a few buildings tower while most stay short.
Insert it behind a points generator and raise the W channel to vary per-instance scale, plus push rotation to ~360 on each axis so stamped copies face random directions.
A new uniform-randomization mode spreads points evenly (a regression that previously couldn't be done); note its Scale knob now writes to point stretch, while W stays free of scaling by default.
Adds per-point colors and scaling to an instanced point set; its random seed is a float, so sweeping it yields smooth deterministic animation rather than discrete reshuffles.

op:Lib.numbers.anim.time.Time.note: Walks the time-source modes: idle/FX time keeps animating while paused, local time follows a [SetTime] remap, playback time ignores remaps, and "last started" time suits damping — pick per situation because each behaves differently when paused or looped.

A short tip on overriding the time that drives an animation: wrap a rendered texture in a command-time operator and feed it a custom time signal (a sine, a remapped random, a beat) to scrub, loop, or jump regions of a timeline non-linearly.
A built-in animation-speed knob avoids wiring a time source, but a "frozen" time mode is what lets a static result stop invalidating and actually cache instead of recomputing every frame.
Its "always evaluated" output flag forces re-evaluation every frame wherever it's wired, which is how a downstream operator keeps reading the live playhead instead of a cached value.

op:Lib.image.use.Blend.note: Two-input compositor with separate colour and alpha blend modes plus per-input colour multipliers; mismatching the two modes (screen colour, normal alpha) is what makes opacity seem ignored.

op:Lib.render.postfx.DepthOfField.note: Needs the depth buffer wired in; set focus distance manually and raise the amount so foreground subjects drift in and out of focus.
Pin it and darken/neutralize the blur so bright out-of-focus elements recede, pulling attention to the sharp center of frame.

op:Lib.point.modify.LinearSamplePointAtt.note: Ignores point world-position and samples a texture/gradient purely by buffer order; right-click the gradient handle to switch interpolation from linear to smooth, and the "blend" stop mode splits the ramp into Photoshop-curve-like zones.

op:Lib.numbers.float.basic.Multiply.note: For spin, feed noise into rotation and multiply its ±1 range up to 360°; lower frequency for slower turns and reduce octaves so the rotation holds a steady speed instead of jittering.

op:Lib.render.shading.SetPointLight.note: Raising decay shrinks the lit area and intensity brightens it; recolor the light for mood — useful for an emissive object that should cast its own colored glow.

op:Lib.numbers.float.process.EaseKeys.note: Pick the curve via the interpolation dropdown (quadratic, exponential, elastic…); the transition duration comes purely from the spacing between keyframes, not a separate speed knob, and a Constant key is the one type left un-eased.

op:Lib.point.transform.IkChain.note: A hard cap on total chain points lives in the solver for the whole buffer, not per chain, to keep an unrolled shader loop from crashing; the angle constraint controls how far each joint may bend.
A GPU FABRIK solver (after Aristidou): feed it a bone chain plus target points and you must raise the per-target Influence above zero, or nothing bends.

op:Lib.numbers.floats.process.ValuesToTe.note: A redo of the bake-list-into-texture op with a clear input-range / clamp / gain-bias / output-range pipeline; use the input range to stretch a tiny value spread (e.g. 0.0–0.003) into a visible, usable texture.

op:Lib.particle.force.MeshVolumeForce.note: Attraction pulls outside particles toward the nearest forward-facing face; repulsion only acts once a particle is detected inside the volume; zero attraction leaves particles untouched. Reflection bounces them off the surface before they enter.

Bounciness below 1 drains energy each bounce, above 1 injects it (things go wild); randomized bounciness and orientation-angle fake a rough surface; moving the collider mesh shoves particles inside and pumps energy into the system.

Pipe any point set into a [ParticleSystem], add this as a force and give it a mesh to collide against; mark its mesh input as required so a missing-input warning shows. Draw the particles before the solid mesh (set draw order so particles write depth first) or they vanish inside it.

ui:Gizmo.note: Enable its gizmo to drag the selection region through the cloud live; scale, stretch and rotate the region to reshape what gets selected.
TiXL is a right-handed Y-up coordinate system (X right, Y up, Z toward camera) — unlike Blender's Z-up; rotations go counter-clockwise. The transform gizmo's coloured axes map directly to X/Y/Z.
Mark a Vector3 parameter as a position/translation in the operator's UI layout so it shows a draggable in-viewport gizmo with a meaningful value range.

op:Lib.point.generate.RadialPoints.note: correct transparency requires drawing back-to-front because the per-pixel write-depth-or-not decision is binary, so a fading sprite must cut off somewhere; order-independent transparency exists but needs a heavy multi-render-target setup comparable to screen-space ambient occlusion.

ui:PerformanceMonitor.note: Read the small numbers under the frame rate, not just the FPS: compute-shader count, triangle count, and draw calls reveal which of the three bottlenecks you've hit. Jittery (not steady-slow) frame times on a laptop mean thermal throttling, not your scene.

Read the frame-time and allocation histograms by their bucket axis: tiny buckets are scaled up so an occasional jitter looks worse than it is; a healthy allocation count stays in the small immediately-freed range, so a spike out of bounds flags a real leak to hunt.

ui:Symbol.note: How example/sample scenes attach to an operator: a symbol named "<OpName>Example(s)" in an Examples namespace is matched by name only (namespace ignored) and surfaces as the operator's how-to.

New MSDF font generator (under utilities) turns any .ttf into a usable signed-distance font written straight into the project's resources/fonts; widen the glyph range for accents/umlauts and raise resolution when you add many glyphs.

op:Lib.image.generate.misc.Sketch.note: internally a fixed-size ring buffer where unused slots are NaN "separator" points that drawing ops skip; the emit cursor wraps around overwriting the oldest particles, the emit count can change freely per frame, and multiple simultaneous emits are distributed across the buffer rather than written as one chunk.

op:Lib.point.modify.PointColorWithField.note: How the new op reads color out of a field per point: call get-field with the "1" selector (0 returns distance, 1 returns color) so the float4 result is the color you write back to the point.

ui:SymbolLibrary.note: How per-project assets, presets and thumbnails are being reorganized into a `.meta` folder (temp/generated ones into git-ignored `.temp`) to stop preset/snapshot confusion.

The pinnable browser groups symbols by namespace; "examples" holds the walk-through how-to operators worth dragging out and double-clicking, and "lib" holds the built-ins sorted by category (field, image, mesh, points…).
Right-click "set thumbnail" on a symbol to capture the current output as its library preview — works for both the operator and its example scene.
Click an operator to jump to its namespace in the library and browse siblings; namespaces like "numbers/logic" group the value-manipulation operators (compare, freeze/hold, LFO) you'd reach for.

Pin an operator, right-click and "set thumbnail" to capture a representative frame; after pressing Update the library shows that preview on hover and while dragging — invaluable when scanning many operators for a VJ set.

op:Lib.point.modify.FilterPoints.note: Count sets the output buffer length and it always tries to fill it; each output cell runs in parallel in a compute shader and infers its source index purely from its own index via start index plus step, wrapping around the source buffer; Step is deliberately a float to allow staggered/grouped Euclidean-style distributions, and Scatter adds per-cell randomization.
Keep only a random subset of points (say 30 of them) so the tall instances scatter sparsely across the grid instead of every cell getting one.
the Step input is a float, so an integer division result must pass through an int-to-float conversion before it will connect; step then takes every Nth source point.
Why you can't shrink a particle buffer cheaply: deleted points are flagged with NaN size rather than removed, since recomputing buffer length needs a slow GPU readback with frame delay.

get longer trails from fewer points by inserting a filter between two particle systems: divide MaxParticleCount for the step count, advance the start index with a frame counter, and use the built-in modulo input to wrap; splitting an existing connection line by clicking it inserts the math op inline.

op:Lib.point.io.LineTextPoints.note: It emits a *buffer of line points* (digit glyphs as strokes), which you push to the GPU and render with [DrawLines]; an internal optimisation that drops empty glyphs is exactly what breaks fixed-width spacing for leading-digit padding.

ui:Field.note: The core F1/F2 explanation: a TiXL point is a fixed 64-byte GPU struct (position, rotation, color, scale) where the unused 4th lanes of two 3-component vectors leave two spare float attributes; every generator, modifier and consumer can write or read F1/F2, making them a universal channel for masks and side effects.
Fields can return not just distances and colors but vectors, and vector fields compose under multiply/transform like any other field.

ui:ParameterWindow.note: The gain/bias vector2 found on many operators is a remap curve: bias shifts the midpoint toward dark or light, gain bends it toward an S-curve (more contrast) or its inverse, letting you reposition and harden a gradient edge playfully instead of editing keys.

How per-parameter snapshots work: instead of flagging a whole operator, right-click individual parameters to expose only those to a snapshot, then capture/recall named states from the empty-input background view.

Per-parameter settings let you group knobs (append "..." to a group name to collapse it by default, while modified params still show), raise display precision, and add a unit suffix that's handy for marking rotations.
On a layer/blend op, drag with the left mouse to set opacity and the right mouse to set luminosity directly on the parameter — a fast shortcut for tinting a fake shadow dark.
Enabling the Vec2 control in the parameter settings lets you drag both components of a paired parameter at once and see the resulting distribution/weighting curve live.

op:Lib.io.midi.MidiRecording.note: A recorded data clip stores per-channel trigger and interval events (MIDI notes, OSC) that can be replayed as simulated device input, so the graph reacts as if the controller were live.

op:Lib.render.postfx.SSAO.note: Adds contact shadows in the crevices between geometry, giving instanced/cluttered scenes much more depth; tame it by lowering opacity or its boost settings if the darkening is too strong.

current shadow options: a projector-style light with halfway-decent single-source shadows, directional draw-with-shadow, and a point-light variant using percentage-closer filtering for slightly blurred edges; ambient occlusion softens shading but is no substitute for real shadows.

ui:OutputSettings.note: The "magic" 0,0 resolution means "inherit the current output resolution"; set a real fixed resolution instead when a texture's aspect ratio must stay square regardless of the window, e.g. for a uniform shadow sprite.
The "magic" 0,0 resolution: take the incoming image's size if one is connected, else the output window's; aspect is preserved by cropping left/right, never top/bottom.

Persistence is split into three layers — the project (operators/animation), the setup (content/surface/output arrangement), and a machine-specific binding of outputs to displays — so whole setups can be switched, and the meter-based size raster makes an object literally A4-sized on the wall.
Create a setup that is never bound to a real display to get a virtual debug overview: one surface with several sub-regions collecting the streams you want to monitor while working.

op:Lib.image.analyze.WaveForm.note: A per-column brightness scope (the film-industry "waveform") that reveals clipping and colour casts the eye misses — use it to spot where highlights blow out before grading, or to neutralise an existing cast channel by channel.
Its vectorscope mode plots a frame's colors on a hue wheel (with a skin-tone line) so you can read a reference's grade — but it only works on a portrait-shaped input.
Its vectorscope plots the image's colours around a hue wheel, exposing how extreme colours snap onto the RGB primaries — the artefact AGX tone-mapping smooths out.
Shows the per-column color distribution of an image (plus a small vectorscope), so you can read which channels are clipping or where a tint sits before grading.

op:Lib.image.color.ToneMapping.note: Pulls clipped super-bright HDR values back into range; the AGX mode blends smoothly toward white instead of letting channels rail to pure R/G/B, avoiding the harsh cut-off look on intense colours.
Compresses over-bright values toward a center curve; the AGX mode desaturates blown-out colors so a clipping bright yellow rounds off instead of flat-lining the waveform into pure primary.
The smartest way to tame over-bright pixels that would otherwise clip: prefer it over simply pulling gain or bloom intensity down, because it compresses highlights rather than crushing them.

ui:ColorEditor.note: TiXL renders into RGBA16, so colours can exceed 1.0; Ctrl-drag a swatch upward past white to make an HDR value (the up-arrow marker), which is what gives [Bloom] and emissive materials their punch.
A pixel keeps its RGB colour even where alpha is 0, so a transparent foreground can still bleed coloured fringes; match fore- and background colour (e.g. both black) to avoid them.
Click the brightness (B) field to toggle modes, and hold Ctrl while dragging to push a colour far past 1.0 into HDR — bright enough to light the scene more than a point light.
A small HDR badge appears once a color's brightness exceeds 1 (Ctrl-drag to push it there); the on-hover mini interpolation curve shows how a gradient blends, exposing OKLab's odd dips through zero.
Swatches surface every color used in the project; Ctrl-clicking a swatch selects and centers all operators that use it, so you can audit and unify a palette across a graph.

ui:LocalTime.note: Time is measured in musical bars, not seconds: four beats per bar, one bar ≈ 2s at 120 BPM, so animation rates expressed in bars stay locked to the beat while still drifting in longer cycles.

op:Lib.image.use.RenderWithMotionBlur.note: Renders a scene over several passes with the time nudged slightly each pass to accumulate true motion blur, which works especially well on fast-moving animated particles; feed it a camera and MSAA-rendered scene.
Accumulates several sub-frame passes at slightly offset times for true long-exposure blur (no post fake); cost scales with pass count, so preview cheap and crank passes only at final render.

ui:Composition.note: Overlay blend mode leaves mid-grey untouched while pushing shadows darker and highlights lighter, acting like a contrast/structure boost when you composite noise or a second image at low opacity.
A maintainer's intro to the project's Discord forum structure and the unstructured meet-up format; context, not an operator lesson.

ui:SkillQuest.note: The new home-panel learning track: a dependency-linked map of levels (basics → images/gradients → points → particles/SDF) you unlock by completing prerequisites, toggleable in settings, with each level a graph you edit to match a reference.

How the guided feature-test window turns each new feature into a step-by-step manual test with pass/skip/fail and Markdown links, doubling as a discoverability tour and a release-acceptance checklist.

A non-linear, map-of-topics learning system where each level shows a hidden target output and you must rebuild it; later levels compare animated value-histories, not just images, so you must reason about the curve rather than just wire nodes.

ui:SkillMap.note: Authoring tools: the Skill-Map editor wires level-unlock dependencies, and the Tour-Point editor attaches Markdown step text and blinking "call-to-action" highlights to specific operators/parameters; tour points round-trip to clipboard as Markdown for editing and LLM grammar passes.
An internal authoring tool for laying out tutorial topics as cells, setting unlock rules (complete one prerequisite vs. all of them) and styles for the quest graph.

ui:ProjectPanel.note: automatic backups save every three minutes and thin out on a binary schedule (recent versions dense, old ones sparse, capped around 16 total), so a corrupted project file no longer crashes the app: pick a backup, optionally archive the broken state for diagnosis, then restore and restart in place.
Install now writes to Program Files like a normal app, so project data lives under Documents (relocatable in settings) and settings/logs/backups under AppData-Roaming.

ui:PlayerExporter.note: Export requires wrapping the graph into a symbol with a texture output (the root level can't have outputs) because the player derives resolution from it; title, author, and the new strip-unused-operators option live in the project's executable settings, and an export button now works from inside the project.
The exporter now scans ahead and pre-compiles upcoming shaders (with shader-source caching so concatenated custom HLSL still hits the cache), removing the playback stutter older preloading missed.

op:Lib.numbers.anim.time.AbletonLinkSync.note: Syncs to any Ableton Link source on the network (Live, Traktor, Bitwig, TouchDesigner, VVVV, DJ gear); unlike MIDI it shares bar-phase, not just BPM, so bar-based timing locks perfectly.

ui:ParameterPopup.note: The combined bias-and-gain curve acts like a tone curve: an S-shape adds contrast (gain), an inverse S flattens it; bias pushes values brighter or darker — one Vec2 parameter covers both shapes across images, distributions and easing.

op:Lib.render.gizmo.Locator.note: A single animated locator acts as one shared position source you can plug into multiple consumers (a mesh and a light) so they always stay co-located.

ui:SplashScreen.note: automatic backups save every three minutes and thin out on a binary schedule (recent versions dense, old ones sparse, capped around 16 total), so a corrupted project file no longer crashes the app: pick a backup, optionally archive the broken state for diagnosis, then restore and restart in place.

op:Lib.numbers.float.process.Accumulator.note: The escape hatch from time-evaluated animation to frame-dependent timing: it integrates an increment each frame, so a live knob (e.g. mouse X) ramps speed smoothly instead of snapping.

op:Lib.io.video.VideoClip.note: Fast-seeking decodes on the CPU into a ~1 GB frame cache so scrubbing forward and back is smooth, while playback-performance mode uses GPU decode plus a compute-shader conversion to play many heavy 4K streams at once.
After the Media-Foundation removal, [PlayVideo] also runs on FFmpeg and exposes an override-time-in-seconds input so you can seek the playhead from the graph.

op:Lib.point.draw.DrawMovingPoints.note: Stretches point billboards in screen space along velocity using camera motion; an option to ignore camera delta is needed for effects (e.g. swimming fish) since billboards must stay screen-facing to avoid zero-width edges.

Stretches each point along its motion into a pill, giving a cheap motion-blur look; the stretch responds to camera rotation too, so even static [GridPoints] streak when you orbit. Only marginally slower than plain point drawing.

op:Lib.image.generate.pattern.ValueRaste.note: Draws a recursively subdividing grid raster whose line density follows image resolution and the chosen value range — the background grid the math quizzes use to plot curves precisely.
A short tip walking through the versatile Raster operator: its presets and knobs, then driving it from an input texture and stacking offset copies into a CMYK-style halftone print effect.

ui:IoView.note: IO recording captures live MIDI/OSC line-input as a data clip of timed events; the point is replaying a recorded live set in the studio to craft visuals against real performance data, not audio production.

op:Lib.numbers.anim.animators.SequenceAn.note: Never drive max-particle-count from a per-frame-changing value: reallocating a large GPU buffer every frame fragments VRAM and can crash; only change buffer size in coarse steps.
Its "set sequential values" fills selected keys with a counting series; start-at and a jump-to-value entry let you begin the run at an arbitrary number like 16.

op:Lib.point.usse.KeepPreviousPointBuffe.note: Hold last frame's point buffer so you can difference positions to get per-point velocity — the basis for velocity-driven scaling and fake motion stretch.
The double-buffer operator behind frame-to-frame velocity: it ping-pongs two buffers so each point's previous position is looked up by ID, which is what any per-point motion effect needs.

op:Lib.field.use.SdfReflectionLinePoints.note: Ray-marches lines through an SDF and reflects them off the surface; raise max-reflections for repeated bounces, and beware it's literal ray-marching — a low step count degenerates, and normal-sampling distance must be tuned to avoid jitter on rough fields.

op:Lib.numbers.anim.vj.GetBpm.note: How beat-locking works: enable "log profile beat syncing" in settings, tap with the V key, and it estimates the best BPM from detected bass transients — robust enough to track a DJ drifting the tempo over time.

op:Lib.render.shading.TextureToCubeMap.note: Always convert an environment image into a cube map before feeding it as the lighting environment — skipping this step can crash the app.

op:Lib.point.draw.DrawBillboards.note: Consolidates the many older point-drawing methods into one flexible operator; its color-variations option can map a point's w attribute to per-point color.
The existing operator for camera-facing (screen-space-aligned) point quads, the thing to reach for instead of hand-rolling an orient-to-camera setup.

Feed it a texture and enable texture-atlas mode to give each point a different sprite cell; build the atlas procedurally by slicing the viewport into a grid and using the loop index to place a character per cell.

op:Lib.numbers.vec3.PerlinNoise3.note: Feed it into a transform's rotation input to drive smooth pseudo-random orientation; keep the output range small (≈0.2) so motion is subtle.
A first points lesson wires a 3D noise into a point's position and a gradient sample into its color/size, demonstrating that point attributes are just inputs you connect like any other.

op:Lib.io.video.PlayVideo.note: Trigger-play a clip from an external event by feeding a stopwatch's elapsed seconds into the video's time input and starting/stopping the watch with the trigger, with looping off so the clip halts at its end.

op:Lib.point.generate.RepeatAtPoints.note: Clone one point set onto every point of another to get spiral/sunflower layouts; because the clones live in each target's local space, a [TransformPoints] offset slides them along their host ring rather than in world space.
Drive many IK chains at once by repeating one line-point chain over a [RadialPoints] ring; you must set "points per chain" to the chain length and strip the separator points.
The orientation axis decides which way the copies fan out; switch it (e.g. to Y) and raise the count so stacked duplicates spread into a usable grid of lines.

op:Lib.point.transform.TransformPoints.note: Pair a point selection with a transform so a squeeze only affects points inside the selected volume, leaving the rest untouched.

Clone one point set onto every point of another to get spiral/sunflower layouts; because the clones live in each target's local space, a [TransformPoints] offset slides them along their host ring rather than in world space.
Apply a move/rotate to every point but scale it by the F1 factor so only masked points actually shift — the canonical "modify only the selection" pattern.

op:Lib.point.draw.DrawLines.note: Rendering a LineTextPoints buffer as strokes is what makes the text usable for transitions and texture-emit tricks, since you then own the raw line geometry.

A new fade-out-if-too-long length cutoff gives a near-free Plexus-style effect: scatter PointsOnMesh, raise the count, and hide long connections so only short links between nearby points survive (also culled cheaply via alpha).

op:Lib.render.basic.Layer2d.note: Composite a soft glowing shape over a scene by scaling a [Layer2d] down and feeding it a [RoundedRect]; crank feathering and tune the aspect ratio for the shape you need.
Add a second texture output to a wrapped operator (right-click → add output, set type to texture), then a 2D layer lets you place that rendered image as a plane in 3D space.

Even an 8x8 texture draws smoothly because sampling defaults to linear filtering (and can visibly wrap at edges); a per-drawer filter option exists only in some operators, prompting the feature request discussed next.

op:Lib.numbers.color.SampleGradient.note: A first points lesson wires a 3D noise into a point's position and a gradient sample into its color/size, demonstrating that point attributes are just inputs you connect like any other.

Inside a custom shader, sample the operator's gradient input by a float coordinate so an exposed parameter slides the sampling point along the ramp, and that parameter can be keyframed or driven by an external value.
Map a beat-synced phase value through a gradient into a colour for an on-beat flash; reversing the gradient flips the attack/decay feel.
Inside a custom point shader, sample a gradient by the field's signed distance (`field.w`) and write it to point colour — distance-banded colouring straight from an SDF.
A new interpolation-override lets you force linear vs. spline blending instead of inheriting it from the gradient type, decoupling output interpolation from the source.
Feed particle age (fx1) into a gradient whose first stop is a sharp bright spike then quick decay, so each particle flashes at birth and dims over its life.

op:Lib.render.transform.Transform.note: Render one scene twice with offset clocks: duplicate the group, feed each copy a different time so the same deterministic animation appears at two phases at once.

op:Lib.field.generate.sdf.HeightMapSdf.note: Turns a single noise channel into terrain as a distance-field operator, pairing cleanly with an SDF-to-color step for a procedural landscape.

op:Lib.field.use.SDFToColor.note: Turns a distance field into a color you can route into DrawMesh, RepeatMeshAtPoints, or DrawMeshAtPoints so every PBR path colorizes from the same field identically.
